title: 6-week Math for AI and ML plan
summary: Linear algebra, probability, statistics, calculus and optimisation for machine learning, with Python and NumPy labs that run and check themselves in the browser. About 6–8 hours a week.

rhythm.text: One lab: read the notes, pass the tests, then a short reading note in your own words and a 20-minute extension in the Playground.
Connect the week to real ML: a lesson or guide, a worked explanation out loud, and a written debrief.
Weekly review: redo one lab from a blank editor, update your formula sheet, and clear due flashcards.

rules: Write the shapes of every array next to the line that creates it.
Check every answer two ways: by hand on a tiny case, and in NumPy.
Seed every random generator so you can repeat a result.
After each lab, explain the idea in three sentences without notation.
Keep a one-page formula sheet and add to it every week.

python: Use import numpy as np and convert inputs with np.asarray(x, dtype=float) so integer inputs do not truncate.
@ is matrix multiplication; * multiplies element by element. Most bugs are one swapped for the other.
Check shapes with x.shape and keep 1-D vectors 1-D; reshape(-1, 1) makes a column only when you need one.
axis=0 collapses rows (one value per column); axis=1 collapses columns (one value per row).
Never form an inverse: use np.linalg.solve or np.linalg.lstsq.
Use rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) for reproducible randomness, not the global np.random functions.
Compare floats with np.allclose or math.isclose, never ==.
Subtract the maximum before np.exp to avoid overflow in softmax and log-sum-exp.

phases.title: Linear algebra
phases.check: Without notes, solve a 3 × 3 system, fit a least-squares line and compute PCA explained variance in NumPy, naming the shape of every array as you go.

phases.title: Probability and statistics
phases.check: Given an A/B result, compute z, the p-value and a 95% interval by hand and in NumPy, and explain a base-rate trap with Bayes’ rule in under two minutes.

phases.title: Calculus and optimisation
phases.check: Code the gradients of a tiny network and of logistic regression, pass a central-difference gradient check, and explain momentum and log-sum-exp out loud.

weeks.title: Vectors, matrices and shapes
weeks.focus: Vectors as data, norms as lengths, dot products as similarity, matrix multiplication as a layer, and broadcasting to work on whole datasets without loops.

tip.python: Print .shape after every line until reading shapes becomes automatic. A (3,) array and a (3, 1) array broadcast very differently.

items.text: Lab: Vector norms: how long is a vector?. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, check that ‖v‖∞ ≤ ‖v‖₂ ≤ ‖v‖₁ holds for 1,000 random vectors from np.random.default_rng(0).
Reading note (10 min): explain why an L1 penalty pushes weights to exactly zero while an L2 penalty only shrinks them.
Lab: Cosine similarity for embeddings. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, normalise five random vectors to length 1 and compute all their pairwise cosine similarities with one matrix multiply.
Lesson: Tokens and embeddings: the units of cost and meaning.
Lab: Matrix multiply and shapes: a linear layer. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, stack two linear layers with a tanh between them and print the shape after each step for a batch of 8 inputs.
Reading note (10 min): write the shapes of X, W, b and the output for a layer that maps 32 examples of 100 features to 10 scores.
Lab: Broadcasting: standardise every feature. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, standardise a training matrix, then apply the same means and spreads to a separate test matrix.
Lesson: Data preparation: reconstruct what was knowable.
Lesson: Transformers: attention, masking, and the KV cache.
Write the shape of Q, K, V, the score matrix QKᵀ and the output for 8 sequences of 128 tokens with 64-dimensional heads.
Redo the linear-layer lab from a blank editor without hints.
Lesson: Neural networks: forward pass, backprop, and when to go deep.
Explain out loud (10 min): what a dot product measures, and why cosine similarity ignores length. Record yourself and listen back.
Written debrief (15 min): which shape or broadcasting mistake did you make this week, and how will you spot it next time?
Weekly review (15 min): start your formula sheet with norms, the dot product, cosine similarity and the shape rule for matrix products.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Refresh Python basics if any syntax slowed you down this week.

weeks.title: Systems, projections, eigenvectors and PCA
weeks.focus: Solving Ax = b and spotting singular matrices, least squares as projection, power iteration for eigenvectors, and PCA through the SVD.

tip.python: Use np.linalg.solve and np.linalg.lstsq rather than inverting. Eigenvectors and singular vectors are only defined up to sign, so compare values or projections, not raw vectors.

items.text: Lab: Solve a linear system (or say it has no single answer). Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, make two nearly identical columns and watch np.linalg.cond(A) grow as they get closer.
Reading note (10 min): describe what “rank below n” means for a feature matrix, with an example of two perfectly correlated features.
Lab: Least squares: fit a line. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, fit the same line with the normal equations and with np.linalg.lstsq, and confirm the answers agree.
Lesson: Regression and classification: choose a target and a loss.
Lab: Projections: the closest point in a subspace. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, check that projecting twice gives the same answer as projecting once, and that the residual is at right angles to every column.
Reading note (10 min): explain why the fitted values of a linear regression are a projection of y.
Lab: Eigenvectors by power iteration. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, compare your power-iteration answer with np.linalg.eigh on a random symmetric matrix, allowing for sign.
Reading note (10 min): say why power iteration converges slowly when the top two eigenvalues are close.
Lab: PCA with the SVD: how much does each direction explain?. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, project a seeded 2-D dataset onto its first component and reconstruct it; measure the error.
Lesson: Clustering: discover structure without inventing labels.
Phase check (45 min): solve a 3 × 3 system, fit a least-squares line and compute PCA explained variance from a blank editor, naming every shape.
Written debrief (15 min): what did you need to look up, and what goes on the formula sheet?
Weekly review (15 min): add the normal equations, projection, eigenvalue and SVD formulas to your sheet, and redo one missed test.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Lesson: Optimization and regularization: control the fit.

weeks.title: Probability, Bayes and simulation
weeks.focus: Conditional probability and Bayes’ rule, expectation and variance, seeded simulation, and the binomial distribution behind rates and counts.

tip.python: When a probability answer surprises you, simulate it: 100,000 seeded draws settle most arguments in a second.

items.text: Lab: Bayes’ rule and base rates. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, plot (print) the posterior for priors from 0.1% to 50% with the same test, and find where it crosses 50%.
Lesson: Imbalance and thresholds: spend a limited review budget.
Lab: Expectation and variance. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, check E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] for two dice by listing all 36 outcomes, and test whether variances add.
Reading note (10 min): explain why variances add for independent variables but not in general.
Lab: Simulation with a seeded random generator. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, rerun the dice simulation with n = 100, 10,000 and 1,000,000 and compare the error with √(p(1 − p)/n).
Reading note (10 min): describe why seeding matters for experiments and tests, and where you would store the seed.
Lab: The binomial distribution. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, compare the binomial pmf for n = 100, p = 0.1 with a normal curve of the same mean and variance.
Reading note (10 min): write the mean and variance of a conversion rate measured on n users, and what doubling n does to its spread.
Lesson: Evaluation: measure the decision you will make.
Write a one-page note: a model flags 2% of transactions and 0.1% are truly fraud; with 90% recall, what share of flags are real? Show the Bayes arithmetic.
Redo the Bayes lab from a blank editor without hints.
Explain out loud (10 min): why a 99%-accurate test can be wrong most of the time it says yes.
Read: Model monitoring: drift, proxies, rollouts and rollback. Note where distributions and base rates appear.
Written debrief (15 min): which probability idea felt least natural, and one example that makes it click?
Weekly review (15 min): add Bayes’ rule, expectation, variance and the binomial pmf to your formula sheet.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Redo one missed lab test from this week, then explain the fix in one sentence.

weeks.title: Estimation, intervals and A/B tests
weeks.focus: Maximum likelihood, standard errors and confidence intervals, the two-proportion z-test, and the bootstrap for metrics with no formula.

tip.python: Say what an interval or p-value means about the procedure before you quote a number. Decide sample sizes before an experiment starts.

items.text: Lab: Maximum likelihood for a normal distribution. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, draw 10 seeded samples from a normal distribution many times and compare the average of the ddof=0 and ddof=1 variances with the truth.
Reading note (10 min): explain why minimising squared error is maximum likelihood under normal noise.
Lab: A confidence interval for a mean. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, simulate 1,000 seeded samples, build a 95% interval from each, and count how many contain the true mean.
Reading note (10 min): explain what “95% confidence” promises about the procedure, and what it does not say about one interval.
Lab: A/B testing: the two-proportion z-test. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, simulate an A/B test with no real difference and peek after every 100 users; count how often p < 0.05 appears at some point.
Read: ML experimentation: offline gates, A/B tests, interleaving.
Lab: The bootstrap: uncertainty by resampling. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, bootstrap a 95% interval for the median of a seeded skewed sample using the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Reading note (10 min): name two metrics where you would use the bootstrap instead of a formula, and why.
Read: LLM evals: golden sets, judges and regression gates. Note how sample size limits what a score difference can tell you.
Lesson: Evaluating LLM systems: golden sets, judges, and noise.
Two prompts score 82% and 85% on 200 eval cases. Write a short note on whether that difference is real, with a z-test.
Phase check (45 min): for 400 of 5,000 against 460 of 5,000, compute z, the p-value and a 95% interval for the lift by hand and in NumPy, then explain a base-rate trap.
Written debrief (15 min): which step slowed you down, and what goes on the formula sheet?
Weekly review (15 min): add MLE, standard error, the z-test and the bootstrap to your formula sheet.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Look ahead: skim the Applied AI and ML plan’s “ML fundamentals and metrics” week (ML engineer track, week 8) to see these ideas in interviews.

weeks.title: Derivatives, gradients and backprop
weeks.focus: Numerical and analytic derivatives, the gradient of a loss, Jacobians of vector functions, and the chain rule run backwards through a small network.

tip.python: Every gradient has the shape of the thing it differentiates. Check new gradient code against a central difference before you trust it.

items.text: Lab: Numerical derivatives. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, plot (print) the error of forward and central differences for h from 1e-1 to 1e-12 and find where rounding takes over.
Reading note (10 min): explain why the central difference is more accurate than the forward difference for the same h.
Lab: The gradient of mean squared error. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, check your MSE gradient against a central difference in every coordinate for a seeded random problem.
Lesson: Optimization and regularization: control the fit.
Lab: Softmax and its Jacobian. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, check every column of the softmax Jacobian against a central difference, and confirm each row adds up to 0.
Reading note (10 min): describe in words what one row of the softmax Jacobian says about raising one score.
Lab: Backpropagation through a tiny network. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, add a gradient check for every entry of dW1 and dw2, then train the tiny net for 100 steps on one example.
Lesson: Neural networks: forward pass, backprop, and when to go deep.
Lesson: Fine-tuning and LoRA: changing behaviour efficiently.
Write a short note: why vanishing gradients happen with many tanh layers, using 1 − tanh² from the backprop lab.
Redo the backprop lab from a blank editor without hints.
Explain out loud (10 min): what backpropagation computes, why it reuses work, and how a gradient check catches bugs.
Read: Training-serving skew: same features offline and online. Note which transforms, like standardising, must match exactly.
Written debrief (15 min): which derivative step was hardest, and how did you check it?
Weekly review (15 min): add the central difference, the MSE gradient, the softmax Jacobian and the backprop equations to your formula sheet.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Redo one missed lab test from this week, then explain the fix in one sentence.

weeks.title: Optimisation, regularisation and a final review
weeks.focus: Gradient descent with momentum, convex quadratic bowls, ridge regularisation, logistic regression from scratch, and stable softmax cross-entropy, then a full review.

tip.python: Stochastic gradient descent uses a random minibatch per step: same update, noisier gradient. Adam adds a per-weight step size to momentum. Both start from the loop you write this week.

items.text: Lab: Gradient descent with momentum. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, count the steps plain descent and momentum need to get within 1e-6 of the minimum for A = diag(10, 1).
Reading note (10 min): explain why a convex loss has no bad local minima, and why neural network losses are not convex.
Lab: Ridge regression in closed form. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, print the ridge weights for λ from 0.01 to 100 on a seeded dataset and watch them shrink.
Lesson: Bias and variance: choose the next experiment.
Lab: Logistic regression by gradient descent. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, train on a seeded two-class dataset with minibatches of 16 (stochastic gradient descent) and compare the loss curve with full-batch descent.
Reading note (10 min): explain why the logistic regression gradient has the same form as the linear regression one.
Lab: Numerically stable cross-entropy. Read the notes, then pass every test.
Extend (20 min): In the Playground, show that the naive and stable versions agree for small logits and that only the stable one survives logits of 1,000.
Lesson: Transformers: attention, masking, and the KV cache.
45-min ML fundamentals mock: explain gradient descent, regularisation and cross-entropy with a whiteboard derivation for each.
Written debrief (15 min): what went well, what to fix, and one formula-sheet entry per miss.
Phase check (45 min): from a blank editor, code logistic regression with a gradient check, then explain momentum and log-sum-exp out loud.
Read: ML pipelines: reproducible training, registries and CI/CD. Note where seeds and versioned data make results repeatable.
Final review (20 min): reread your formula sheet end to end and redo the two labs you found hardest.
Flashcards: clear today’s due cards.
Next: continue with the Applied AI and ML plan; its ML engineer track covers ML fundamentals and production systems in weeks 8 and 9.
Or: the Forward Deployed Engineer plan puts these skills to work on customer data and LLM apps.
